To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mentoring programs for Indigenous young people at risk are a promising initiative because they are culturally appropriate and can assist in building protective factors that result indeterminants of positive life outcomes.

mentoring programs are a promising strategy for improving the outcomes for Indigenous youth at-risk, particularly if they are part of broader programs that include other strategies to improve outcomes for Indigenous youth.

mentoring programs for Indigenous youth are a promising intervention for improving outcomes and reducing contact with juvenile and criminal justice systems; and mentoring programs are a particularly promising intervention for Indigenous youth because they fit well with Indigenous teaching, learning and cultural values, and they can help to build and strengthen community connections.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effectiveness of mentoring programs for Indigenous youth in Australia; how Indigenous mentoring programs can be improved and expanded to meet the needs of Indigenous youth at risk of disengagement and/or offending behaviour; the role of mentoring programs in the broader context of youth justice programs for Indigenous youth; and the effectiveness of mentoring in reducing contact with the youth justice system.

the following questions: What are the most effective ways to implement mentoring programs for at-risk Indigenous youth? What are the best practices in mentoring programs for Indigenous youth? What is the evidence that mentoring programs for Indigenous at-risk youth can reduce contact with juvenile justice?

the nature of the mentoring relationship and the role of mentors; the characteristics of effective programs and the role of the mentor within the program; the outcomes of mentoring programs, particularly those targeting Indigenous youth at risk of offending; and the role of mentoring within a range of programs targeting Indigenous youth at-risk.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Mentoring programs for Indigenous young people at risk of engaging in antisocial behaviours can have a positive effect in improving their behavioural, academic and employment outcomes.
mentoring is an effective way to help at-risk Indigenous youth to develop the skills, knowledge and attitudes needed to make positive choices in their lives.

there is evidence to support mentoring programs for Indigenous youth as an effective strategy in reducing risk factors and increasing protective factors that may lead to a reduction in the number of Indigenous young people engaging in criminal behaviours and/or being incarcerated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

mentoring programs can be effective in improving behavioural, social, and vocational outcomes for Indigenous youth, and can reduce the likelihood of Indigenous youth coming into contact with the juvenile justice system.
Indigenous mentoring programs can be an effective strategy in addressing the needs of Indigenous young people at risk.
the more structured and formal the mentoring program, the less effective it is likely to be in improving outcomes for young people at risk of antisocial behaviour.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mentoring is not a ‘one-size-fits-all’ intervention
mentoring can be a useful strategy to support Indigenous young people at risk, and to help build protective factors that can lead to positive outcomes for them and their communities.
mentoring programs can be effective in helping young people to avoid antisocial behaviour, and that they can be adapted to suit Indigenous contexts and needs.
